html:
The Massachusett were an Algonquian people whose homeland covered much of present-day Greater Boston, along the Charles and Neponset rivers and Massachusetts Bay. The colony and state are named after them; the name comes from a place name meaning "at the great hill".

They farmed maize, beans and squash and fished the coast. An epidemic from 1616 to 1619, brought by European ships, killed most of them before the English came. The Puritan settlers of the 1630s then took the emptied lands around Boston. The missionary John Eliot gathered converts into "praying towns" and printed a Bible in their language in 1663, the first Bible printed in the Americas. In King Philip's War, the praying Indians were interned on Deer Island, where many died. See Massa-adchu-es-et and the neighbouring Wampanoag.
